chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: triangles from three lengths first, then triangles from angles, then altitudes and kinds of triangles. Every rule is reached by building a triangle and asking when it cannot be built, so a rule such as the triangle inequality is a finding and not a fact to memorise.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves one question open: what happens when three corner points lie on a straight line. The compass construction and the triangle inequality arrive only after the student has tried to build triangles.

points.title: When a triangle cannot be built
points.text: For lengths, for two sides and an angle, and for two angles and a side, the chapter asks when the construction fails. Each failure leads to a rule: the triangle inequality, an angle below 180 degrees, and two angles that add to less than 180 degrees.

points.title: Parallel lines explain the angles
points.text: One line drawn through a vertex parallel to the opposite side explains why two angles must add to less than 180 degrees, how to find the third angle, and why the three angles always add to 180 degrees.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the figure is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

concepts.concept_name: A frame of three beams

content.text:
A triangle is the most basic closed shape. As we know, it consists of:
three corner points, that we call the vertex of the triangle, and
three line segments or the sides of the triangle that join the pairs of vertices.
Triangles come in various shapes.
Observe the symbol used to denote a triangle and how the triangles are named using their vertices. While naming a triangle, the vertices can come in any order.
The three sides meeting at the corners give rise to three angles that we call the angles of the triangle. For example, in ∆ABC, these angles are ∠CAB, ∠ABC, ∠BCA, which we simply denote as ∠A, ∠B and ∠C, respectively.

content.text:
1. Picture three wooden beams of a shed roof, nailed together at their ends to make a triangle frame. The three nails are the corners, called vertices, and the beams are the sides.
2. Make a guess before the next step: if the top nail is pressed down until all three nails lie on one straight line, do we still have a triangle?
3. A triangle can be named with its vertices in any order: ∆ABC, ∆BCA and ∆CAB are the same triangle. Its angles are ∠A, ∠B and ∠C.

concepts.concept_name: Building with a ruler alone

content.text:
7.1 Equilateral Triangles
Among all the triangles, the equilateral triangles are the most symmetric ones. These are triangles in which all the sides are of equal lengths. Let us try constructing them.
Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm.
How did you construct this triangle and what tools did you use? Can this construction be done only using a marked ruler (and a pencil)?
Constructing this triangle using just a ruler is certainly possible. But this might require several trials. Say we draw the base, let us call it AB, of length 4 cm, and mark the third point C using a ruler such that AC = 4 cm. This may not lead to BC also having a length of 4 cm. If this happens, we will have to keep making attempts to mark C till we get BC to be 4 cm long.
How do we make this construction more efficient?

concepts.concept_name: Two arcs find the third corner

content.text:
Recall solving a similar problem in the previous year using a compass (in the Chapter 'Playing with Constructions'). We had to mark the top point of a 'house' which is 5 cm from two other points. The method we used to get that point can also be used here.
After constructing AB = 4 cm, we can do the following.
Step 1: Using a compass, construct a sufficiently long arc of radius 4 cm from A. The point C is somewhere on this arc. How do we mark it?
Step 2: Construct another arc of radius 4 cm from B. Let C be the point of intersection of the arcs.
The construction ensures that both AC and BC are of length 4 cm. Can you see why?
Step 3: Join AC and BC to get the required equilateral triangle.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm, and explain why AC and BC are both 4 cm.
1. Draw the base AB of length 4 cm.
2. Step 1: with the compass set to 4 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
3. Step 2: keep the compass at 4 cm, put the point on B, and draw a second arc that crosses the first.
4. Mark the crossing point C. It is on the arc from A, so AC = 4 cm, and on the arc from B, so BC = 4 cm.
5. Step 3: join AC and BC. All three sides are 4 cm.
Answer: An equilateral triangle ABC with AB = BC = CA = 4 cm

concepts.concept_name: Constructing a triangle of sides 4, 5 and 6

content.text:
7.2 Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
How do we construct triangles that are not equilateral?
Construct a triangle of sidelength 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
As in the previous case, this triangle can also be constructed using just a marked ruler. But it will involve several trials.
How do we construct this triangle more efficiently?
Choose one of the given lengths to be the base of the triangle: say 4 cm. Draw the base. Let A and B be the base vertices, and call the third vertex C. Let AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.
Like we did in the case of equilateral triangles, let us first get all the points that are at a 5 cm distance from A. These points lie on the circle whose centre is A and has radius 5 cm. The point C must lie somewhere on this circle. How do we find it?
We will make use of the fact that the point C is 6 cm away from B. Construct an arc of radius 6 cm from B.
Let us summarise the steps of construction, noting that constructing full circles is not necessary to get the third vertex.
Step 1: Construct the base AB with one of the side lengths. Let us choose AB = 4 cm.
Step 2: From A, construct a sufficiently long arc of radius 5 cm.
Step 3: From B, construct an arc of radius 6 cm such that it intersects the first arc.
Step 4: The point where both the arcs meet is the required third vertex C. Join AC and BC to get ∆ABC.

Worked example: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
1. Step 1: draw the base AB = 4 cm.
2. Step 2: with the compass set to 5 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
3. Step 3: set the compass to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc.
4. Step 4: the crossing point is C. It is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B. Join AC and BC.
5. Check with the ruler: AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
Answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Why the crossing point is the third vertex, and isosceles triangles

content.text:
The required point C is one of the points of intersection of the two circles.
The reason why the point of intersection is the third vertex is the same as for equilateral triangles. This point lies on both the circles. Hence its distance from A is the radius of the circle centred at A (5 cm) and its distance from B is the same as the radius of the circle centred at B (6 cm).
We have seen that triangles having all three equal sides are called equilateral triangles. Those having two equal sides are called isosceles triangles.

Worked example: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm and say what kind of triangle it is.
1. Take the side of 6 cm as the base AB.
2. From A draw an arc of radius 4 cm, and from B draw an arc of radius 4 cm. They cross at C.
3. C is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B, so AC = BC = 4 cm.
4. Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.
Answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Construct (triangles from three sides)

content.text:
Construct (triangles from three sides): Construct triangles having the following sidelengths (all the units are in cm): (a) 4, 4, 6 (b) 3, 4, 5 (c) 1, 5, 5 (d) 4, 6, 8 (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5. Say what kind of triangle each is.
1. Each set satisfies the check: the two shorter lengths add to more than the longest (4 + 4 > 6, 3 + 4 > 5, 1 + 5 > 5, 4 + 6 > 8, 3.5 + 3.5 > 3.5), so each triangle can be built.
2. For each set draw the longest side as the base, then an arc of one of the other lengths from each end.
3. (a) 4, 4, 6 has two equal sides: isosceles. (b) 3, 4, 5 has three different sides: scalene. (c) 1, 5, 5 has two equal sides: isosceles, with a very short base.
4. (d) 4, 6, 8 has three different sides: scalene. (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5 has three equal sides: equilateral.
Answer: All five can be built: (a) isosceles, (b) scalene, (c) isosceles, (d) scalene, (e) equilateral

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q1: A circle is drawn with its centre marked, and some points are marked on the circle. Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles.
1. Mark the centre O and two points P and Q on the circle. Join OP, OQ and PQ.
2. OP and OQ are both radii of the same circle, so OP = OQ and triangle OPQ is isosceles.
3. Choosing P and Q so that PQ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
4. Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take P and Q, then take R halfway between them on the circle, so that RP = RQ.
Answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q2: Two circles of the same size have centres A and B, and each circle passes through the centre of the other. Then three circles of the same size have centres A, B and C, and each circle passes through the centres of the other two. Use the points on the circles and/or their centres to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.
1. Two circles: each passes through the other's centre, so the radius equals AB. Let C and D be the two points where the circles cross.
2. C is on the circle at A, so AC = AB, and on the circle at B, so BC = AB. All three sides of triangle ABC are equal: it is equilateral. In the same way triangle ABD is equilateral.
3. AC = AD because both are radii of the circle at A, so triangle ACD is isosceles; triangle BCD is isosceles in the same way.
4. Three circles: A, B and C are the centres and every pair of centres is one radius apart, so triangle ABC is equilateral. Each pair of circles crosses in two points, and each crossing point together with those two centres gives another equilateral triangle.
5. Any point on a circle with the centre and another point on the same circle gives an isosceles triangle, as in the single circle.
Answer: Triangles ABC and ABD are equilateral, and ACD and BCD are isosceles; with three circles ABC is equilateral and each crossing point forms more equilateral triangles

content.text:
Are Triangles Possible for any Lengths?
Can one construct triangles having any given sidelengths? Are there lengths for which it is impossible to construct a triangle? Let us explore this.
Construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm.
What is happening? Are you able to construct the triangle?
Here is another set of lengths: 2 cm, 3 cm, and 6 cm. Check if a triangle is possible for these sidelengths.
Try to find more sets of lengths for which a triangle construction is impossible. See if you can find any pattern in them.
We see that a triangle is possible for some sets of lengths and not possible for others. How do we check if a triangle exists for a given set of lengths? One way is to actually try to construct the triangle and check if it is possible. Is there a more efficient way to check this?

content.text:
1. Predict first: with a base of 8 cm, can an arc of 3 cm from one end ever meet an arc of 4 cm from the other end?
2. The two arcs reach only 3 cm and 4 cm from the two ends of an 8 cm base, which is 7 cm in all. They fall short and never cross, so there is no third vertex.
3. The same happens for 2, 3 and 6: 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6.
4. Look for the pattern in other failing sets, such as 1, 2, 5 or 4, 5, 10: the two shorter lengths together are less than the longest.

content.text:
Worked example: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm, and say what happens to the arcs.
1. Take 8 cm as the base AB. Draw an arc of 3 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B.
2. The arc from A reaches 3 cm along the base and the arc from B reaches 4 cm back, which covers 3 + 4 = 7 cm of the 8 cm. They do not meet.
3. For 2, 3 and 6, take 6 cm as the base. The arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm cover 2 + 3 = 5 cm of the 6 cm and do not meet.
4. In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6.
Answer: No triangle can be built for 3, 4, 8 or for 2, 3, 6: the arcs never meet

concepts.concept_name: A direct path and a roundabout path

content.text:
Triangle Inequality
Consider the lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm. Does there exist a triangle having these as sidelengths?
To tackle this question, let us study a property of triangles. Imagine a small plot of plain land having a tent, a tree, and a pole. Imagine you are at the entrance of the tent and want to go to the tree. Which is the shorter path: (i) the straight-line path to the tree (the red path) or (ii) the straight-line path from the tent to the pole, followed by the straight-line path from the pole to the tree (the yellow path)?
Clearly, the direct straight-line path from the tent to the tree is shorter than the roundabout path via the pole. In fact, the direct straight-line path is the shortest possible path to the tree from the tent.
Will the direct path between any two points be shorter than the roundabout path via a third point? Clearly, the answer is yes.

content.text:
Worked example: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
1. Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
2. Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
3. 30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
4. The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
Answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

concepts.concept_name: The triangle inequality: 10, 15, 30 and 3, 3, 7

content.text:
Can this understanding be used to tell something about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm?
Let us suppose that there is a triangle for this set of lengths. Remember that at this point we are not sure about the existence of the triangle but we are only supposing that it exists. Let us draw a rough diagram.
If this triangle were possible, then the direct path between any two vertices should be shorter than the roundabout path via the third vertex. Is this true for our rough diagram?
Let us consider the paths between B and C. Direct path length = BC = 10 cm. Roundabout path length = BA + AC = 15 cm + 30 cm = 45 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.
Let us now consider the paths between A and B. Direct path length = AB = 15 cm. Roundabout path length = AC + CB = 30 cm + 10 cm = 40 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.
Finally, consider paths between C and A. Direct path length = CA = 30 cm. Roundabout path length = CB + BA = 10 cm + 15 cm = 25 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? In this case, the direct path is longer, which is absurd. Can such a triangle exist? No.
Therefore, a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist.
We are thus able to see without construction why a triangle for the set of lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist. We have been able to figure this out through spatial intuition and reasoning.
Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm? Verify your answer by construction.
In the rough diagram, is it possible to assign lengths in a different order such that the direct paths are always coming out to be shorter than the roundabout paths? If this is possible, then a triangle might exist. Is such rearrangement of lengths possible in the triangle?

content.text:
You would have realised that using a rough figure and comparing the direct path lengths with their corresponding roundabout path lengths is the same as comparing each length with the sum of the other two lengths. There are three such comparisons to be made.
Given three sidelengths, what do we need to compare to check for the existence of a triangle?
When each length is smaller than the sum of the other two, we say that the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality. For example, the set 3, 4, 5 satisfies the triangle inequality whereas, the set 10, 15, 30 does not satisfy the triangle inequality.
We have seen that lengths such as 10, 15, 30 that do not satisfy the triangle inequality cannot be the sidelengths of a triangle.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q1: We checked by construction that there are no triangles having sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm; and 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm. Check if you could have found this without trying to construct the triangle.
1. For 3, 4 and 8: the longest is 8 and the other two add to 3 + 4 = 7.
2. 8 > 7, so the direct length is longer than the roundabout length: no triangle.
3. For 2, 3 and 6: the longest is 6 and the other two add to 2 + 3 = 5.
4. 6 > 5, so again no triangle. No construction was needed.
Answer: Yes: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6, so neither set makes a triangle

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q3 (Try This)

content.text:
Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q3 (Try This): For the set 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm, two comparisons hold (10 < 15 + 30 and 15 < 10 + 30) but the third does not (30 > 10 + 15). Will there always be at least two comparisons where the direct length is less than the sum of the other two? Explore for different sets of lengths. Is it possible to tell which lengths will immediately be less than the sum of the other two, without calculations? [Hint: Consider the lengths in increasing order.]
1. Write the lengths in increasing order: a, b, c with a ≤ b ≤ c.
2. The length c is the longest, so a < b + c is true because b + c is already at least c, which is at least a. Also b < a + c, because a + c is at least c, which is at least b.
3. Only the comparison for c, c < a + b, can fail.
4. Test with 7, 10, 15: 7 < 10 + 15 = 25 and 10 < 7 + 15 = 22 hold, and the longest check 15 < 7 + 10 = 17 holds too. For 10, 15, 30 the first two hold and only the longest check, 30 < 25, fails.
5. So at least two comparisons always hold, and the two that always hold belong to the two shorter lengths. Only the longest length needs a check.
Answer: Yes, at least two comparisons always hold: the two shorter lengths are always less than the sum of the other two, so only the longest length needs to be checked

concepts.concept_name: Seeing the circles for 4, 5 and 8

content.text:
Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm?
This satisfies the triangle inequality: 8 < 4 + 5 = 9
This means that all the direct path lengths are less than the roundabout path lengths. Does this confirm the existence of a triangle?
If one of the direct path lengths had been longer, we could have concluded that a triangle would surely not exist. But in this case, we can only say that a triangle may or may not exist.
For the triangle to exist, the arcs that we construct to get the third vertex must intersect. Is it possible to determine that this will happen without actually carrying out the construction?
Visualising the construction of circles
Let us imagine that we start the construction by constructing the longest side as the base. Let AB be the base of length 8 cm. The next step is the construction of sufficiently long arcs corresponding to the other two lengths: 4 cm and 5 cm.
Instead of just constructing the arcs, let us complete the full circles. Suppose, we construct a circle of radius 4 cm with A as the centre. Now, suppose that a circle of radius 5 cm is constructed, centred at B. Can you draw a rough diagram of the resulting figure?
Note that in the figure below, AX = 4 cm and AB = 8 cm. So, what is BX? Does this length help in visualising the resulting figure?
Since BX = 4 cm, and the radius of the circle centred at B is 5 cm, it is clear that the circles will intersect each other at two points.
What does this tell us about the existence of a triangle? The points A and B along with either of the points of intersection of the circles will give us the required triangle. Thus, there exists a triangle having sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm.

4. BX = 4 cm is less than the radius 5 cm of the circle at B, so the circle at B goes beyond X, into the circle at A. The circles cross at two points.
5. Either crossing point with A and B gives a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm.

Worked example: Check the lengths 6, 7 and 12 by comparing only the longest length with the sum of the other two, and then check the other two comparisons to see that they hold.

4. All three hold, so the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality.

content.text:
Figure it Out (which lengths make a triangle), Q1: Which of the following lengths can be the sidelengths of a triangle? Explain your answers. Note that for each set, the three lengths have the same unit of measure. (a) 2, 2, 5 (b) 3, 4, 6 (c) 2, 4, 8 (d) 5, 5, 8 (e) 10, 20, 25 (f) 10, 20, 35 (g) 24, 26, 28
1. Compare the longest length with the sum of the other two.
2. (a) 2 + 2 = 4 < 5: no triangle. (b) 3 + 4 = 7 > 6: a triangle. (c) 2 + 4 = 6 < 8: no triangle.
3. (d) 5 + 5 = 10 > 8: a triangle. (e) 10 + 20 = 30 > 25: a triangle. (f) 10 + 20 = 30 < 35: no triangle.
4. (g) 24 + 26 = 50 > 28: a triangle.
Answer: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)

concepts.concept_name: Three cases for two circles

content.text:
Will triangles always exist when a set of lengths satisfies the triangle inequality? How can we be sure?
We can be sure of the existence of a triangle only if we can show that the circles intersect internally (as in Fig. 7.5) whenever the triangle inequality is satisfied. But are there other possibilities when the two circles are constructed? Let us visualise and study them.
The following different cases can be conceived: Case 1: Circles touch each other. Case 2: Circles do not intersect. Case 3: Circles intersect each other internally.
Note that while constructing the circles, we take (a) the length of the base AB = longest of the given length (b) the radii of the circles to be the smaller two lengths.
Which of the above-mentioned cases will lead to the formation of a triangle? Clearly, triangles are formed only when the circles intersect each other internally (Case 3).
Let us study each of these cases by finding the relation between the radii (the smaller two lengths) and AB (longest length).
Case 1: Circles touch each other at a point. For this case to happen, sum of the two radii = AB or sum of the two smaller lengths = longest length
Case 2: Circles do not intersect internally. For this case to happen, what should be the relation between the radii and AB? It can be seen from the figure that, sum of the two radii < AB or sum of the two smaller lengths < longest length
Case 3: Circles intersect each other. AB is composed of one radius and a part of the other. So, sum of the two radii > AB, or sum of the two smaller lengths > longest length

content.text:
1. Predict first: if the two radii add up to exactly the base, where do the circles meet?
2. Touch: the radii exactly fill the base, so the circles meet at one point on the base, and the three points are on one line. This is the answer to the question of three vertices on a line.
3. Miss: the radii add up to less than the base, so a gap is left between the circles.
4. Cross: the radii add up to more than the base, so the circles overlap and meet at two points.

content.text:
Worked example: On a base AB, take two circles whose radii are the two smaller lengths. For the sets 3, 5, 8 and 2, 5, 8 and 5, 6, 8 say whether the circles touch, miss or cross, and whether a triangle exists.
1. 3, 5, 8: the base is 8 and the radii are 3 and 5. The radii add to 3 + 5 = 8, equal to the base, so the circles touch at one point. No triangle.
2. 2, 5, 8: the radii add to 2 + 5 = 7, less than 8, so the circles miss. No triangle.
3. 5, 6, 8: the radii add to 5 + 6 = 11, more than 8, so the circles cross in two points. A triangle exists.
Answer: 3, 5, 8: touch, no triangle; 2, 5, 8: miss, no triangle; 5, 6, 8: cross, a triangle exists

concepts.concept_name: A complete test for a triangle

content.text:
Can we use this analysis to tell if a triangle exists when the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality?
If the given lengths satisfy the triangle inequality, then the sum of the two smaller lengths is greater than the longest length. This means that this will lead to Case 3 where the circles intersect internally, and so a triangle exists.
How will the two circles turn out for a set of lengths that do not satisfy the triangle inequality? Find 3 examples of sets of lengths for which the circles: (a) touch each other at a point, (b) do not intersect.
Frame a complete procedure that can be used to check the existence of a triangle.
Conclusion: If a given set of three lengths satisfies the triangle inequality, then a triangle exists having those as sidelengths. If the set does not satisfy the triangle inequality, then a triangle with those sidelengths does not exist.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality, which of the three cases happens?
2. The inequality says the two smaller lengths add to more than the longest, which is Case 3: the circles cross and a triangle exists.
3. If the inequality fails, the sum is equal to the longest length (the circles touch) or less (the circles miss): no triangle either way.
4. Touching examples: 2, 3, 5; 4, 4, 8; 1, 6, 7. Missing examples: 1, 2, 5; 3, 3, 9; 2, 4, 10.

content.text:
Worked example: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths can make a triangle, and use it on 3.5, 6 and 9, and on 4, 7 and 11.
1. Step 1: find the longest length.
2. Step 2: add the other two lengths.
3. Step 3: if the sum is more than the longest, a triangle exists; if the sum is equal or less, it does not.
4. 3.5, 6, 9: the longest is 9 and 3.5 + 6 = 9.5. 9.5 > 9, so a triangle exists.
5. 4, 7, 11: the longest is 11 and 4 + 7 = 11. The sum equals the longest, so the circles touch and no triangle exists.
Answer: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q1: Check if a triangle exists for each of the following set of lengths: (a) 1, 100, 100 (b) 3, 6, 9 (c) 1, 1, 5 (d) 5, 10, 12
1. (a) The longest is 100 and 1 + 100 = 101 > 100: a triangle exists.
2. (b) The longest is 9 and 3 + 6 = 9, equal to 9: the circles touch, so no triangle.
3. (c) The longest is 5 and 1 + 1 = 2 < 5: no triangle.
4. (d) The longest is 12 and 5 + 10 = 15 > 12: a triangle exists.
Answer: Triangles exist for (a) and (d); not for (b) (circles touch) or (c)

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q2: Does there exist an equilateral triangle with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does there exist an equilateral triangle of any sidelength? Justify your answer.
1. For 50, 50, 50 the longest is 50 and the other two add to 50 + 50 = 100.
2. 50 < 100, so the triangle inequality holds and an equilateral triangle exists.
3. For any side length s the other two add to s + s = 2s, and s < 2s as long as s is more than zero.
4. So the circles always cross: an equilateral triangle exists for every side length. It can be built with the two-arcs method of the first topic.
Answer: Yes: 50 < 50 + 50, and in general s < s + s for any side length s above zero

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q3 (Try This)

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q3 (Try This): For each of the following, give at least 5 possible values for the third length so there exists a triangle having these as sidelengths (decimal values could also be chosen): (a) 1, 100 (b) 5, 5 (c) 3, 7. See if you can describe all possible lengths of the third side in each case, so that a triangle exists with those sidelengths. For example, in case (a), all numbers strictly between 99 and 101 would be possible.
1. The third length x must be less than the sum of the other two, and the other two lengths must each be less than the sum of x and the remaining length.
2. (a) 1 and 100: x < 1 + 100 = 101, and 100 < 1 + x gives x > 99. So x is strictly between 99 and 101: for example 99.5, 100, 100.5, 99.9 and 100.9.
3. (b) 5 and 5: x < 5 + 5 = 10, and 5 < 5 + x gives x > 0. So x is strictly between 0 and 10: for example 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
4. (c) 3 and 7: x < 3 + 7 = 10, and 7 < 3 + x gives x > 4. So x is strictly between 4 and 10: for example 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
5. In general, for two lengths p and q, the third length is strictly between the difference of p and q and the sum of p and q.
Answer: (a) strictly between 99 and 101, for example 99.5, 100, 100.5; (b) strictly between 0 and 10, for example 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; (c) strictly between 4 and 10, for example 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
